p: The bronze figures here were sculpted by Gutzon Borglum, of Mount Rushmore fame. They honor the soldiers of North Carolina, who would advance across these fields in greater numbers — and fall in greater numbers — than the men of any other state in Lee's army.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 4, North Carolina Memorial, paragraph 3 of 3

p: Where Lee watched the charge. From near this spot, Confederate commander Robert E. Lee watched the climax of the battle unfold. The towering statue depicts Lee astride his horse Traveller, gazing east across the very ground his men would be ordered to cross.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 5, Virginia Memorial, paragraph 1 of 3

p: On the afternoon of July 3, some 12,000 Confederates stepped out of these trees and started across nearly a mile of open field toward the Union center — the assault remembered as Pickett's Charge. Lee had convinced himself that one massive blow to the middle of the line could win the battle.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 5, Virginia Memorial, paragraph 2 of 3

p: It was a tragic miscalculation. The field before you became a killing ground, and the failure of the charge marked the turning point not only of the battle but, many believe, of the war itself.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 5, Virginia Memorial, paragraph 3 of 3

p: Longstreet's hidden march. On the afternoon of July 2, Confederate General James Longstreet massed his divisions along this stretch of Seminary Ridge, using these woods to screen his movements from watching Union eyes.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 6, Pitzer Woods, paragraph 1 of 3

p: His objective was Meade's left flank, far to the south — a sweeping attack meant to roll up the Union line from the bottom. The march to get into position was long and exhausting, and the delay it caused would have real consequences.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 6, Pitzer Woods, paragraph 2 of 3

p: When Longstreet's assault finally crashed forward, it ignited some of the most savage fighting of the entire war, at places whose names would pass into legend: Devil's Den, the Wheatfield, the Peach Orchard, and Little Round Top.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 6, Pitzer Woods, paragraph 3 of 3

p: The storm breaks, 4 p.m. Here on Warfield Ridge, Longstreet's Confederates surged forward against the Union left — a flank that General Dan Sickles had pushed dangerously far ahead of the rest of the army, against orders.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 7, Warfield Ridge, paragraph 1 of 3

p: Confederate General John Bell Hood's division swung toward the Round Tops and Devil's Den, hunting for the very end of the Union line so they could turn it. Hood himself was badly wounded almost as soon as the attack began.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 7, Warfield Ridge, paragraph 2 of 3

p: What followed was three hours of ferocious combat across the southern half of the battlefield — a churning series of attacks and counterattacks that would decide whether Lee could shatter Meade's army on its second day.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 7, Warfield Ridge, paragraph 3 of 3

p: The anchor of the Union left. This rocky hill was the hinge of the entire Union line — and on July 2 it was nearly left undefended. Meade's chief engineer, Gouverneur Warren, rode up, grasped the danger in an instant, and rushed troops to the summit just minutes before the Confederates struck.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 8, Little Round Top, paragraph 1 of 3

p: At the far end of the line, the 20th Maine under Colonel Joshua Chamberlain held the very tip of the Union army. Running low on ammunition and about to be overwhelmed, Chamberlain ordered a desperate downhill bayonet charge that swept the attackers back.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 8, Little Round Top, paragraph 2 of 3

p: Had Little Round Top fallen, Confederate guns could have raked the length of the Union line. Its defense became one of the most celebrated episodes of the battle — and the view from its boulders is among the most striking on the whole field.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 8, Little Round Top, paragraph 3 of 3

p: The bloody Wheatfield. Few places on the battlefield saw more concentrated horror than this single farm field. Through the afternoon it changed hands again and again as fresh troops from both sides were fed into the fight.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 9, The Wheatfield, paragraph 1 of 3

p: Charge met countercharge in a swirling, smoke-choked struggle that trampled the wheat flat and left the ground strewn with more than 4,000 dead and wounded men. Survivors would remember it ever after simply as “the bloody Wheatfield.”

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 9, The Wheatfield, paragraph 2 of 3

p: By evening the field belonged to the Confederates — but at a staggering cost, and the Union line behind it on Cemetery Ridge still held firm.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 9, The Wheatfield, paragraph 3 of 3
